  MISSION STATEMENT
  The mission of the City of Monterey Park is to provide excellent service, foster growth
  and opportunity, and create a joyous and collaborative environment.

  LAND ACKNOWLEDGMENT
  We would like to acknowledge that the land we inhabit today was once known as
  Tovangaar, the home of the Gabrieleño-Tongva people. We show our respect to the
  Gabrieleño-Tongva people, as well as all Indigenous people, past, present, and future,
  and honor their labor as original caretakers of this land. We commit to uplifting the
  Gabrieleño-Tongva people, invite you to acknowledge the history, and join us in caring
  for this land.

GENERAL INFORMATION
Documents related to an Agenda item are available to the public in the City Clerk’s Office located at 320
West Newmark Avenue, Monterey Park, CA 91754, during normal business hours and the City’s website
at www.montereypark.ca.gov/AgendaCenter/City-Council-17.

The public may watch the meeting live on the city’s cable channel MPKTV (AT&T U-verse, channel 99
or Charter Communications, channel 182) or by visiting the city’s website at
www.montereypark.ca.gov/133/City-Council-Meeting-Videos. Per the Americans with Disabilities Act, if
you need special assistance to participate in this meeting, please call City Hall at (626) 307-1359 for
reasonable accommodation at least 24 hours before a meeting. Council Chambers are wheelchair
accessible.

PUBLIC PARTICIPATION
You may speak up to 5 minutes on an/each Agenda item. You may combine up to 2 minutes of time with
another person’s speaking. No person may speak more than a total of 10 minutes. The Mayor and City
Council may change the amount of time allowed for speakers. Written Communication will be accepted
up  to  24  hours  before  the  meeting  by  completing  an  online  form  at
www.montereypark.ca.gov/writtencomm.

While all comments are welcome, the Brown Act does not allow the City Council to take action on any
item not on the agenda. The Council may briefly respond to comments after Public Communications is
closed. Persons may, in addition to any other matter within the City Council's subject-matter jurisdiction,
comment on Agenda Items at this time. If you provide public comment on a specific Agenda item at this
time, however, you cannot later provide comments at the time the Agenda Item is considered.

 TO:  The Honorable Mayor and City Council
 FROM:  Diana Garcia, Assistant City Manager
 SUBJECT:  Update on Permanent Memorial Efforts and Request Direction to
  Engage a Consultant to Lead Community Engagement Process

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Receiving and filing this update on the permanent memorial process, including
  recent survey results;
  2. Providing direction to staff to engage a consultant to facilitate a broad-based
  community engagement process to guide the design and location of the permanent
  memorial;
  3. Taking such additional, related actions as may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
Over the past several months the MPK Hope Resiliency Center conducted an initial
community survey to gather preliminary input on the establishment of a permanent
memorial to honor the victims of the January 21, 2023 tragedy. Survey results show
community support for creating a memorial, with a preference for an outdoor environment
and a garden setting.

To move forward, staff recommends engaging a consultant to lead a broad-based
community engagement process. Staff is seeking Council’s feedback on the proposed
community engagement process utilizing the assistance of a consultant.

BACKGROUND:
In response to the mass shooting on January 21, 2023, which claimed 11 lives, the City
of Monterey Park has worked to support the community’s mental health and healing in
variety of ways, from providing support and counseling in City facilities, to assisting with
the opening of the MPK Hope Resiliency Center and the establishment of the MPK
Healing Fund, to holding events to bring community members together to remember and
honor victims and survivors.

Since the shooting, the City has also considered the establishment a permanent memorial
to honor the victims and support community healing. City staff has worked closely with
Chinatown Service Center (CSC) to support the community’s healing. In September 2024,
Nina Loc, CSC’s Chief Behavioral Health Officer and then Director of the MPK Hope
Resiliency Center, informed staff that CSC was initiating discussions with the family
members of victims and the survivors about their sentiments on a permanent memorial.

March 19, 2025

As a part of this feedback process CSC staff also created a survey to gather additional
feedback from victims and survivors about the permanent memorial.

After approximately three months of discussions and surveying the family members and
survivors, CSC staff pushed the survey out in January 2025 to the greater community to
gather input. The City has shared the survey via social media, the City website, and
promotion in our City facilities and at public events.

   Survey Results

Between November 2024 and February 2025, a total of 222 questionnaires were
completed as part of the community outreach effort to gather input on the creation of a
permanent memorial in Monterey Park (Attachment 1). Of these, 152 were physical
submissions collected at various outreach events, and 70 were submitted online. Some
individuals declined to complete the questionnaire, sharing that they felt the topic did not
pertain to them.

The survey data was collected from a wide range of sources to ensure broad community
participation. It was made available online, and paper copies were distributed at
community events, including the Lunar New Year Festival, at the Library and at dance
events at the Langley Center.

Overall, the survey showed support for establishing a permanent memorial. 82.6% of
respondents (181 out of 219) indicated they are in favor of building a memorial in
Monterey Park. A portion of respondents shared other perspectives, with 7.8% (17 out of
219) expressing they are not interested, and 9.1% (20 out of 219) indicating they are
uncertain.

When asked about the preferred setting for the memorial, the majority of respondents
(84.3%, or 177 out of 210) favored an outdoor environment, while 14.3% (30 out of 210)
preferred an indoor location.

   Memorial Planning Process

In addition to expressing support for the memorial itself, 30% of respondents indicated an
interest in participating in planning efforts to help shape the memorial's design and
purpose. These results confirm clear interest from the community in being directly
involved in any memorial’s planning and development.

Staff recommends engaging a consultant to facilitate a broad-based community
engagement process. This approach provides flexibility for participants, allowing
individuals to engage at their comfort level while ensuring broad participation, and a
structured yet inclusive decision-making process similar to a strategic or master planning
effort. A broad-based community engagement process will also allow for meaningful
participation from a wide range of stakeholders without the challenges of maintaining a

  Page 7 of 229
 Staff Report
Page 3 of 3
March 19, 2025

structured committee such as quorum issues, turnover, and sensitivity of member
selection and appointment. The consultant will:

  •  Design and implement an inclusive outreach process.
  •  Utilize various engagement tools, such as surveys, community meetings, focus
  groups, and individual interviews.
  •  Leverage the knowledge and experiences of various stakeholders, including
  community leaders, victims' families and survivors.
  •  Ensure accessibility, language support, and diverse community representation.
  •  Help synthesize community input into a clear vision for the memorial’s design and
  location.
  •  Maintain openness and transparency in all decisions, ensuring the community is
  informed and involved throughout the project.

If the approach is approved by City Council, staff will begin seeking out a consultant and
will request funding at a future Council meeting to support this effort.

  DATE: January 15, 2025

 TO:  The Honorable Mayor and City Council
 FROM:  Diana Garcia, Assistant City Manager
 SUBJECT:  Update on the Work of the January 21 Memorial Ad Hoc Subcommittee
  and Consideration of Further Action

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Receiving and filing this report on the permanent memorial process;
  2. Providing further direction to staff on next steps; and
  3. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
The January 21 Memorial Ad Hoc Subcommittee made progress in exploring options for
a permanent memorial to honor the victims of the 2023 mass shooting and learning more
about how other communities affected by mass violence have addressed this important
work. Staff is updating Council on the progress of the Subcommittee and asking for further
direction from City Council on next steps.

BACKGROUND:
In response to the tragic mass shooting on January 21, 2023, which claimed 11 lives, the
City of Monterey Park has worked to support the community’s mental health and healing
in variety of ways, from providing support and counseling in City facilities, to assisting with
the opening of the MPK Hope Resiliency Center and the establishment of the MPK
Healing Fund, to holding events to bring community members together to remember and
honor victims and survivors.

Since the shooting, the City has also considered the establishment a permanent memorial
to honor the victims and support community healing.

  Ø Preliminary Research and the First 12 Months

At the City Council meeting on September 6, 2023, in order to help guide initial discussion
and inform any next steps the Council was provided with preliminary research on
memorials for six mass casualty events in the United States: Sandy Hook Elementary
School (Sandy Hook, Connecticut), Route 91 Harvest Music Festival (Las Vegas,
Nevada), Inland Regional Center Attack (San Bernardino, California), Borderline Bar and

  Page 18 of 229
 Staff Report
Page 2 of 4
January 15, 2025

Grill Shooting (Thousand Oaks, CA), PULSE Nightclub (Orlando, Florida), and the
Virginia Tech Shooting (Blacksburg, Virginia) .

The City Council initially considered the six different memorial committees, their
composition, methods of community input, responsibilities, timelines and budgets. At that
point, the discussion was preliminary, as mass casualty experts that staff had consulted
with advised that it was very early in the healing process to begin to make decisions on a
permanent memorial.

On January 21, 2024, the City held a vigil to mark one year since the shooting and to
allow the community to come together in unity and support. The event incorporated
Buddhist chanting, prayer, a Tongva blessing, music from Mark Keppel’s string quintet,
and remarks from City of Monterey Park elected officials, and survivors, family and
community members. The City has a vigil to mark the second year since the shooting
scheduled for January 21, 2025 at 6:00 p.m. in front of Monterey Park City Hall.

  Ø Council-Established Ad Hoc Subcommittee

In May 2024, staff brought the permanent memorial discussion back to City Council, and
an ad hoc subcommittee to further consider the issue of a permanent memorial in
Monterey Park was established. The subcommittee is comprised of two members of the
City Council: Mayor Thomas Wong and Councilmember Henry Lo.

Since its establishment, the subcommittee, along with City Manager Inez Alvarez and
Assistant City Manager Diana Garcia, has met with individuals who have personal
experience setting up memorials in the aftermath of mass casualty incidents, including
Tennille Pereira, who has worked to support the community in the aftermath of the Route
91 shooting in Las Vegas and Anita Ahuja, who has helped communities respond to mass
violence for over twenty years. The subcommittee has considered various topics
associated with the establishment of a memorial, including funding, outreach and
communication, staffing, committee composition, professional facilitators, memorial
design, request for proposal processes, and project timelines.

  Ø Partnership with Chinatown Service Center

Since the mass shooting, City staff has worked closely with the Chinatown Service Center
(CSC) to support the community’s healing. In September 2024, Nina Loc, CSC’s Chief
Behavioral Health Officer and then Director of the MPK Hope Resiliency Center, informed
staff that CSC was initiating discussions with the family members of victims and the
survivors about their sentiments on a permanent memorial. As a part of this feedback
process CSC staff also created a survey to gather additional feedback from victims and
survivors about the permanent memorial.

After approximately three months of discussions and surveying the family members and
survivors, CSC staff pushed the survey out in January 2025 to the greater community to

gather input. This survey will run through the end of February 2025. The City has shared
the survey via social media, the City website, and promotion in our City facilities, and will
distribute paper survey at the Bruggemeyer Library and the Langley Senior Center.

Initial survey results indicate a general interest in establishing a memorial, though 5% of
respondents indicated that they are "uncertain", and another 5% are "not interested” in
establishing a memorial. Respondent largely support an outdoor garden memorial, or a
mural, memorial wall or sculpture.

  Ø Next Steps

In cities affected by mass casualty events, outreach efforts to establish a permanent
memorial—such as surveys, meetings, and town hall events—are often led by Resiliency
Center staff who maintain close ties to the impacted communities. These efforts help
ensure that the memorial reflects the desires and needs of those most affected.

In Monterey Park, staff from the MPK Hope Resiliency Center are continuing to survey
residents through at least February 2025 to gauge interest and gather input on the
potential establishment of a permanent memorial. City staff are currently assisting in
promoting this survey to ensure broad community participation.

Subcommittee and staff recommend that the City Council provide direction on the next
steps in this process. Possible options include:

  •  Allowing Additional Outreach: Waiting until outreach efforts are concluded to
  gain further input from the community.
  •  Designating a Memorial Committee: Provide direction regarding the creation of
  a committee; or delegation of oversight to members of the City Council or other
  entity.
  •  Dedicating City Property: Identifying and dedicating a City property or space for
  a memorial.
  •  Fundraising Efforts: Directing a designated entity to initiate fundraising for the
  memorial with a set timeframe for these efforts and based on funds collected
  establish next steps.

FISCAL IMPACT:
There is no immediate fiscal impact associated with this discussion.

 SUBJECT:  Discussion of Establishing a Memorial Committee for the January 21st
  Mass Shooting Incident

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Receiving and filing the staff report and attachments;
  2. Discussing the establishment an independent Memorial Committee for the January
  21st Mass Shooting Incident;
  3. If desirable, providing additional staff direction; and
  4. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
On January 21st, the City of Monterey Park experienced a tragic mass shooting incident
that resulted in the loss of 11 lives and left the community deeply affected. The City
recognizes the need to honor the memory of the victims and create a space for healing,
remembrance, and reflection for the entire community.

In response to this tragic event, there has been public interest and support for the creation
of a permanent memorial that will serve as a place for residents and visitors to pay their
respects and remember the lives that were lost. The memorial would serve not only as a
tribute to the victims but also as a symbol of resilience and unity for the Monterey Park
community. Communities affected by similar tragedies often establish committees that
tackle the fundraising, outreach and planning for permanent memorials, which consist of
a diverse group of community members, stakeholders, and experts in memorial design
and public spaces.

Initial research on the memorials for six mass casualty events in the United States is
attached for Council to review and to help guide initial discussion. Council may provide
direction on next steps and/or request this item to be put on the agenda for discussion at
future meetings.

BACKGROUND:
Other communities affected by mass violence have formed commissions to establish
permanent memorials to their victims. Attachment 1 outlines staff’s initial research on the
processes undertaken in response to six tragedies: Sandy Hook Elementary School

BACKGROUND:
On November 5, 2024, voters adopted Measure BE which updated the structure of the
City’s business license tax to be based on a business’s gross receipts. The measure was
adopted with a 70.46% voter approval. On December 18, 2024, City Council adopted a
scaled BLT schedule for businesses earning over $25,000,000 annually. The scale
reduces the BLT owed by higher yielded gross revenue businesses in the City, while still
maintaining an equitable tax across all city businesses.

Like many cities, the City of Monterey Park imposes a local business tax to help fund
municipal services within the community. The City uses these revenues for City services
such as police patrol, fire suppression, parks, recreation, maintenance services, library
services and senior programs. The business license tax is not regulatory; it is for revenue
generation only.

The Monterey Park Municipal Code (“MPMC”) § 5.08.010 requires that any person (which
includes businesses) owning or transacting business in the City to obtain a license,
regardless of where the business is physically located.

MPMC § 5.12.200 establishes BLT for unclassified businesses. The City Council found
that it was in the public interest to establish a BLT that is lower than that authorized in
MPMC § 5.12.200 for businesses that operate within the City exclusively during City-
hosted events. Such an event would include, for example, the annual Lunar New Year
Event.

If adopted, the draft Resolution would both suspend the business license tax during the

 Ralph Andersen & Associates conducted a Total Compensation Survey for the City of Monterey Park.
The survey was conducted consistent with prior compensation surveys and included the following
parameters:

  •  12 survey agencies that directly compete with the City and serve as a reliable indicator of the
  market trends
  •  93 survey job classifications (job titles)
  •  The collection of salary range, cash benefit, and insurance benefit data to allow for both a base
  salary range analysis and total compensation analysis of key benefits.

The purpose of the compensation survey is to obtain data and inform City decision makers in labor
bargaining, budgeting, and optimizing the City’s ability to recruit and retain employees.

The survey results were analyzed statistically with comparisons of City salary ranges and benefits with
the median (50th percentile) of the market agencies. The market median is a useful comparison
representing the middle of the market. Establishing a market anchoring point for the City’s
compensation is a policy decision that may involve trade-offs such as the need to compete with peer
agencies versus budget limitations that may limit salary and benefit levels. Some agencies may
establish salary and benefits levels above or below median depending on policy goals.

In summary, the City’s salary ranges are at or above the labor market median. When benefits are
considered in the analysis, there is not a significant change in market position except for a few job
classifications/employee groups. The following provides more detailed findings:

  •  The City’s Executive Management, Mid-Management, Confidential, and SEIU groups are above
  market median on average when salary ranges are compared (ranging from +4.6% to +7.6% on
  average); when benefits are added, there is a slight but insignificant improvement in market
  position primarily due to City paid longevity and deferred compensation benefits.
  •  The City’s Firefighter group is also slightly above market median, with a +3.9% relationship to
  median when base salary is compared and a +2.1% comparison to median when benefits are
  added.
  •  The City’s Fire Management, Police Captains, Police Mid-Management, and Police job
  classifications are at or below median when salary ranges are compared (ranging from +1.6% to
  -6.6% compared to median); when benefits are added, the market relationships shift to -1.4%
  to -5.7% compared to median.

The survey findings described above represent data for the 2024-25 fiscal year as of January 2025 and
provide a point-in-time picture of the City’s salary and benefits. Market changes for subsequent fiscal
years typically begin in July of each year.

BACKGROUND:
In 2016 the City awarded a contract to RKA Consulting Group to develop the PS&E for
road improvements and the construction of landscaped medians and the project was
placed on hold due to project funding and timing issues.

The City, along with Los Angeles County and the neighboring cities of Montebello and
Rosemead, submitted for grant funding for the installation of bike lanes and related
improvements along Potrero Grande.

The project encompasses several following jurisdictions including City of Monterey Park,
City of Rosemead, City of Montebello and Unincorporated Los Angeles County (Los
Angeles County Public Works). The project limits are on:
•  W. 1st St. from Vancouver Ave. to Atlantic Blvd.,
•  Atlantic Blvd. from W. 1st St. to W. Riggin St.,
•  W. Riggin St. from Atlantic Blvd. to Fulton Ave.,
•  Fulton Ave. from E. Riggin St. to E. Markland Dr.,

The project brings connectivity between major activity and transportation centers through
construction of long segments of missing sidewalks, ADA compliant curb ramps, and
crosswalk enhancements. There is also a lack of regional bicycle connectivity between
San Gabriel Valley cities, with many bicycle facilities dropping at city boundaries. The
project proposes to expand alternative modes of travel by increasing existing bicycle
transportation network and enhancing pedestrian facilities. These measures will increase
connectivity between homes, jobs, public transit, schools, and recreational resources for
a variety of road users in unincorporated South San Gabriel, and the Cities of Monterey
Park, Montebello and Rosemead.

Riggin Street, in the City of Monterey Park, has existing bicycle facilities, which
includes Class III and Class II bike routes from Atlantic Blvd. to Wilcox Ave. The
proposed bike facilities will extend and provide continuity and a connection between
the existing bicycle facilities along Riggin Street and to the future bicycle lanes along 1st
Street in East Los Angeles, which is part of the Metro Gold Line Eastside Access Phase
II project. Missing sidewalks along Potrero Grande Drive discourage active
transportation by forcing pedestrians to walk in the street. This project will provide
greater accessibility and mobility for pedestrians, cyclists and transit users providing
safe and productive alternative modes of travel.

The City delayed the design and construction of the road improvements and median
construction until the signal improvements at Potrero Grande and Market Place, and
Potrero Grande and Markland were completed. The proposed improvements were critical
to align with the proposed improvements along Potrero Grande. This project required
Caltrans review and approval and inspection and faced delays. At this time, the signal
improvement construction is completed. In addition, Southern California Edison was
improving the parkway along Potrero Grande. These improvements were also completed.

The Director requested that RKA provide a proposal to complete the improvement plans
for Potrero Grande. The goal is to design and bid both the road improvement and median
project at the same time as the 1st-Riggin-Potrero Grande Corridor Project. Having the
same contractor perform the work is expected to result in cost savings and will eliminate
any necessary coordination between two contractors if the City was to bid the two projects
separately. As a result, the Director requested from RKA a proposal for the development
of the PS&E for the 1st-Riggin-Potrero Grande Corridor Project -MAT Cycle 1.

It is recommended that City Council authorize the City Manager to execute an agreement
with RKA Consulting Group in an amount not to exceed $407,055, for the preparation of
PS&E for Potrero Grande Renovation (Road and median) Project and for the preparation
of PS&E for 1st-Riggin-Potrero Grande Corridor Project -MAT Cycle 1.

This Project meets the City’s goal to maintain, build and modernize infrastructure and

improve public transportation, pedestrian and bicyclist mobility and safety.

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Authorizing the City Manager to execute a Professional Services agreement with
  Mark Thomas, for the preparation of Plans, Specifications and Engineer’s
  estimates (PS&E) for Garvey Capacity Improvements Project in an amount not to
  exceed $1,348,896; and
  2. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
The City was awarded funding through the Los Angeles County Metropolitan
Transportation Authority (“LACMTA”) Project ID# MR2.1.1.21 and FTIP #LA9918883.
The City released a Request for Proposals (“RFP”) and received four proposals for the
preparation of PS&E for Monterey Pass Road Complete Street Project. Following an
extensive selection process that included interviews of four firms, the Public Works
Director (“Director”) selected Kimley-Horn and Associates, Inc. as the most qualified
consultant for this work. The Garvey Capacity Improvements Project necessitates
qualifications closely aligned with those required for the Monterey Pass Complete Street
Project. To facilitate the timely completion of the Garvey Capacity Improvements Project’s
design, the Director has determined that Mark Thomas is the most suitable candidate for
the City’s award. The Director requested a proposal from Mark Thomas for the proposed
work on Garvey Avenue, and a cost proposal was negotiated. The Director requests City
Council approval to enter into an agreement with Mark Thomas in an amount not to
exceed $1,348,896, for the preparation of PS&E for Garvey Capacity Improvements
Project (the “Contract”).

BACKGROUND:
The City received funding from LACMTA to fund the development and construction of the
Garvey Avenue Capacity Improvements project, from West Atlantic Boulevard to New
Avenue. The Project is approximately 1.7 miles in length.

The Project location is depicted below.

The Project is an eligible SR-710 North Corridor Mobility Improvement approved by the
Metro Board of Directors on April 4, 2024, and contributes to mobility and operational
benefits in the SR-710 corridor, between 1-10 and I-210, consistent with the purpose and
need of the 710 Gap Closure project.

The Project is anticipated to:

  •  Improve public transit/bus flow
  •  Improve pedestrian mobility and safety
  •  Improve/promote bicycle use by evaluating routes and usage on adjacent streets
  and in the surrounding area.
  •  Improve traffic flow, reduce congestion, thus reduce emission of green-house
  gases. (Traffic congestion on roads not only increases the fuel consumption but
  consequently leads to increase in carbon dioxide emissions, outdoor air pollution
  as well as increase in the exposure time of the passengers.)
  •  Promote electric vehicle use by providing EV charges for public use, thus reducing
  emission of green-house gases.

The City released a Request for Proposals (“RFP”) and received four proposals for the
preparation of PS&E for Monterey Pass Road Complete Street Project.

Following an extensive evaluation process that included interviews and presentation of
all firms, the Director selected Kimley-Horn and Associates, Inc. as the most qualified
consultant for this work. Mark Thomas was ranked a close second in the evaluation
process.

The Garvey Capacity Improvements Project necessitates qualifications closely aligned
with those required for the Monterey Pass Complete Street Project. Pursuant to
Resolution No. 2025-R3 declaring a local emergency, the City Council authorized the City
Manager to by-pass the standard procurement policies. As a result, to facilitate the timely
completion of the Garvey Capacity Improvements Project’s design, the Director has
determined that Mark Thomas is the most suitable candidate for the City’s award. The
Director requested a proposal from Mark Thomas for the proposed work on Garvey
Avenue, and a cost proposal was negotiated.

It is recommended that City Council authorize the City Manager to execute an agreement
with Mark Thomas in an amount not to exceed $1,348,896, for the preparation of PS&E
for Garvey Capacity Improvements Project.

2024-25 STRATEGIC PLAN GOAL:
This Project meets the City’s goal to maintain, build and modernize infrastructure and
facilities to support the current and future needs of our city and community as it aims to
improve public transportation, pedestrian and bicyclist mobility and safety, improve traffic
flow and reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

FISCAL IMPACT:
The Contract cost will not exceed $1,348,896. The Contract funds are budgeted as part
of Capital Improvement Project (“CIP”) No. 96052, and will be funded through SR 710
grant funding.

  DATE: March 19, 2025
  AGENDA ITEM NO: Consent Calendar - 3I

 TO:  The Honorable Mayor and City Council
 FROM:  Shawn Igoe, Director of Public Works
 SUBJECT:  Waive Spirit Bus Fares for Earth Day on April 22, 2025

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Waiving Spirit Bus fare for riders for one week, starting on April 21, 2025 through
  April 25, 2025, in celebration of Earth Day; and
  2. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
It is recommended that City Council waive the fare to the Spirit Bus starting on Monday,
April 21, 2025, through April 25, 2025 in celebration of Earth Day which will be celebrated
globally on April 22, 2025. Free rides on the Spirit Bus will promote public transportation
and reduce traffic and the City’s carbon footprint through the reduction of automobile
emissions. This action will support the City’s Going Green initiative to encourage the
community to consider environmentally friendly activities such as using alternative forms
of transportation. The Spirit Bus fare was also waived last year for an entire week, as
requested by City Council, in honor of Earth Day 2024.

In 2023, the City waived Spirit bus fare for one day and there were 167 riders that
benefited from waived fares for that day. In 2024, the City waived fare for the entire week
and saw an 81% increase in ridership that week compared to the prior year. A total of
1,535 riders used Spirit Bus for Earth Day week 2024, compared to 844 riders that used
the bus on the same week in 2023.

FISCAL IMPACT:
The Spirit Bus fare is $0.25 per passenger per boarding. Based on last year’s ridership
counts, the estimated impact of waiving bus fares for one week in honor of Earth Day is
approximately $383.75. This revenue loss will be from General Funds.

 SUBJECT:  Annual Weed Abatement Protest Hearing

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Opening the continued public hearing, receiving public comment, closing the
  public hearing;
  2. Adopting a Resolution declaring at weeds, brush, rubbish and refuse upon or in
  front of specified property in the city are a seasonal and recurrent public
  nuisance, and declaring its intention to provide for abatement; and/or
  3. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.
CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act):
Adopting of this Resolution is exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act
(“CEQA”) under CEQA Guidelines § 15061 (b)(3) because it can be seen with certainty
that there is no possibility that the Resolution may have a significant effect on the
environment.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
The County of Los Angeles Department of Agriculture Commissioner/Weights and
Measures (Weed Abatement Division) submitted to the City the annual Weed Abatement
Declaration List and resolution declaring that weeds, brush, rubbish, refuse and dirt
maintained on certain private properties in the City are a public nuisance. At the regular
City Council meeting on February 5, 2025, the City Council adopted Resolution No. 2025-
R4 approving the 2025 Weed Abatement Declaration List as posted by the County. By
adopting the Resolution, the Council declared its intention to provide for the abatement
of said nuisances. To complete the process, the Council must hold a protest hearing to
allow parcel owners identified on the Declaration List an opportunity to object to their
inclusion thereon.

BACKGROUND:
The County identified 1,614 improved or unimproved parcels requiring abatement in the
2025 Declaration List. The County mailed notices on or about January 6, 2025 to the
recorded owner of each parcel included in the list declaring at their parcel is in existing,
future, or “potential” hazard. The County advised that it considers a parcel a future or
“potential” hazard if the parcel is not completely landscaped or irrigated and there is a

potential for weed growth. The Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors established an
inspection fee of $53.14 for the 2025 abatement cycle.

Parcel owners who received notices from the County can challenge their parcels inclusion
on the list by attending the protest hearing. Parcel owners can request Council to remove
their parcels from the list if they feel their parcel is not in violation or that the County has
erred by including the parcel on the list. The City Manager also has the authority to
remove parcels from the list, thus the City Council may defer any requests for removal to
the City Manager for further consideration.

The County advised staff that if parcel owners want their parcel to be removed from the
Declaration List, the County will conduct re-inspection of the parcel to determine if, in fact,
the parcel is not in violation or a potential hazard, or that an error has been made. Upon
completion of the re-inspection of the parcel, the County will advise the City of its findings.
When a parcel is re-inspected and found to be in violation or a potential hazard, the
County will remove the parcel from the deletion list. The deletion list will allow the re-
inspection fee of $53.14 to be waived.

The County advised the City that March 26, 2025 is the last day that the City can
request or the County can authorize removal of a parcel from the Declaration List. If
the City Council elects to remove a parcel from the Declaration List and the parcel
becomes a nuisance at a later date, the City will have to place that parcel on an
individual declaration list and will have to hold an individual protest hearing for each
parcel.

The following is a schedule of the Weed Abatement process:
March 26, 2025  Deadline for the City to authorize removal of a property from the
  Declaration List.

April 1, 2025  County will begin clearance operations on unimproved (vacant)
  parcels.

May 14, 2025  Deadline for all improved parcels to attain compliance that
  responded to the County via response cards. County will begin
  compliance inspections.

August 6, 2025  Weed Abatement Charge List Hearing of Weed Abatement Costs
  directing the County to collect these costs through property tax
  billings.

FISCAL IMPACT:
The City of Monterey Park has been contracting with the County of Los Angeles since
1992 for weed abatement services. No fiscal impacts are anticipated to affect actual
expenditures or revenues. Furthermore, no redirection of available staff time, supplies or
services will be required.

 SUBJECT:  Public Hearing Pursuant to Government Code Section 3502.3
  Concerning Vacancies and Recruitment and Retention Efforts

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Conducting a public hearing to present the status of vacancies and recruitment
  and retention efforts in accordance with Government Code section 3502.3; and
  2. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
Effective January 1, 2025, Government Code Section 3502.3 requires public agencies to
hold at least one public hearing per fiscal year to discuss the City’s workforce vacancies
and recruitment and retention efforts. The City’s recognized employee associations were
provided timely advance notice of the public hearing.

BACKGROUND:
Government Code section 3502.3 requires the City to present the status of vacancies and
recruitment and retention efforts during a public hearing before the City’s governing body
at least once per fiscal year. This presentation must be made prior to the adoption of a
final budget if the governing body will be adopting an annual or multiyear budget during
the fiscal year in which the public hearing is held. The City’s recognized employee
associations may make a presentation during the public hearing concerning vacancies
and recruitment and retention efforts. The City has eight bargaining units. Additional
reporting obligations exist if vacancies within a single bargaining unit meet or exceed 20
percent of the total number of authorized positions, at the affected bargaining unit’s
request. The vacancy reports for each association are attached.

   Recruitment and Retention Efforts

The City has taken steps to address recruitment efforts in the recent years. In June 2022,
the City Council declared an employment emergency to address vacancies. Coming out
of the COVID-19 pandemic, there was a limited pool of qualified candidates and growing
vacant positions. After the expiration of the employment emergency, the City revised the
recruitment process by amending the City’s Personnel Rules and Regulations. The
revised recruitment process provides flexible options to fill civil service positions. These

  Page 189 of 229

March 19, 2025

efforts assisted in reducing the approximately 70 vacant positions in June 2022 to
approximately 30 vacancies currently.

Human Resources/Risk Management staff continue to work with each
department/division to discuss different ways to advertise and attract candidates for
vacant positions/recruitments. Civil service recruitments typically consist of multiple steps
which are used to help narrow down the pool of applicants in a fair and impartial process
based on minimum qualifications to perform the essential duties of the position (i.e. written
exam, performance testing, and/or oral interview).

Hiring departments are aware of retention efforts for current employees, and often provide
promotional recruitments rather than open recruitments, such as providing additional time
for staff to be trained and have an opportunity to participate. For example, the Fire
Department provided opportunities for current Firefighters to attend paramedic school to
be qualified to fill the vacant Firefighter/Paramedic positions.

Moving forward, staff will be tracking and capturing additional recruitment details and data
related to the regulations of the new Government Code.

FISCAL IMPACT:
There are no identifiable fiscal impacts associated with conducting the public hearing
required under Government Code section 3205.3. There are potential fiscal impacts to
address recruitment and retention issues for future budget and bargaining considerations
which will be presented to the City Council as needed.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
The City’s 6th cycle (2021-2029) Housing Element (“HE”) and Revised Monterey Park
2040 Land Use Element (“LUE”) establish a vision and long-term goals for development,
housing, and redevelopment within the City. The attached Ordinance implements the LUE
and HE by: (1) requiring replacement housing for development projects that displace
existing units; (2) resolving inconsistencies in the administrative use permit approval
requirements for alcohol related uses; (3) aligning the MPMC with volatile State accessory
dwelling unit laws; and (4) establishing the residential incentive zone allowing certain
housing developments without any discretionary approvals.

BACKGROUND:
On November 3, 2020, City voters approved Measure JJ which adopted the Revised
Monterey Park 2040 Land Use Element (“LUE”). Pursuant to Ordinance No. 2198, the
City Council is authorized to take all appropriate action to implement the LUE.

In March of 2023, the California State Department of Housing and Community
Development (HCD), certified the City’s HE. Government Code § 65583(c) requires that
cities include programs which set forth a schedule of actions the local government is
undertaking or intends to undertake to implement the policies and achieve the goals and
objectives of the HE. Included in the HE were several programs which proposed
consistency between the General Plan and MPMC to help encourage the production of a
variety of housing types and at various affordability levels. The attached ordinance
implements several of these programs (further described below) and continues the City’s
efforts of harmonizing the LUE, HE, and MPMC.

  Ø Accessory Dwelling Units (“ADUs”)
HE Program 12 and LUE Implementation Program 2 require MPMC amendments to
implement State ADU and junior accessory dwelling unit (“JADU”) mandates. Since the
City’s adoption of the current ADU and JADU provisions in the MPMC in 2018 and 2020,
State ADU and JADUs laws have changed each year to further encourage new
construction. The attached ordinance will amend the MPMC to implement the State
mandate and ensure consistency among all ADU and JADU provisions in the MPMC.

  Ø Replacement Housing
HE Program 13 requires that the City amend the MPMC to require the replacement of
units affordable to the same or lower income level as a condition of development on a
nonvacant site. The attached Ordinance establishes a new section within the MPMC
(section 21.02.260) implementing the aforementioned requirement, consistent with the
requirements set forth in Density Bonus law.

  Ø Residential Incentive Zone (“RIZ”)

California Housing Element law requires cities and counties to identify specific land and
properties that are suitable for residential development in order to accommodate the
jurisdiction’s Regional Housing Need Allocation (“RHNA”), commonly known as a sites
inventory. The sites inventory, contained in the Housing Element must include sufficient
sites and demonstrate that these sites can accommodate housing at various income
levels. Sites in the City’s inventory includes both vacant and non-vacant properties.
Government Code § 65583 and HE Program 10 require the City to approve certain
qualifying housing development projects ministerially when the site on which its proposed
is a non-vacant site included in one previous housing element inventory or a vacant site
included in two previous housing element inventories. The attached ordinance will
implement HE Program 10 by establishing the RIZ and changing the zoning designation
for those specific properties included in the current sites inventory of the HE that were
also listed in prior HE cycles to accommodate housing to RIZ.

Maps of the affected properties including their existing zoning designations are included
as part of the Ordinance (Attachment 1). Any existing overlay zones, such as Planned
Development Overlays or Senior Citizen Housing Overlays that exist on the affected
properties will remain in place.

The RIZ zone is an opportunity to allow developers who propose residential projects
under certain conditions to be approved ministerially. However, such developments must:

  •  Have 20% of residential units that are affordable to low-income households;
  •  Restrict affordable units for a term of not less than 55 years;
  •  Replace affordable units lost in the construction of a new project;
  •  Feature specified amenities; and
  •  Meet objective design standards.

  Ø Alcohol Sales and Use

To address inconsistencies in the MPMC and streamline alcohol sales for businesses,
the City Council authorized accessory use of on-site and off-site alcohol sales subject to
an Administrative Use Permit (“AUP”) as part of the Business Recovery Program
(Ordinance No. 2203). The attached ordinance will amend the MPMC to eliminate
conflicting provisions throughout the MPMC.

2024-25 STRATEGIC PLAN GOAL:
The attached ordinance satisfies the 2024-25 Strategic Plan Goal to “Strengthen our local
economy and enhance housing opportunities” by achieving the goals and programs set
forth in the HE, reducing barriers to encourage housing development, and supporting
economic growth in the City.

SECTION 11: Renumbering. All provisions of the MPMC affected by this Ordinance are
appropriately renumbered.

SECTION 12: Electronic Signatures. This Ordinance may be executed with electronic
signatures in accordance with Government Code § 16.5. Such electronic signatures will
be treated in all respects as having the same effect as an original signature.

SECTION 13: Construction. This Ordinance must be broadly construed to achieve the
purposes stated in this Ordinance. It is the City Council’s intent that the provisions of this
Ordinance be interpreted or implemented by the City and others in a manner that
facilitates the purposes set forth in this Ordinance.

SECTION 14: Summaries of Information. All summaries of information in the findings,
which precede this section, are based on the substantial evidence in the record. The
absence of any particular fact from any such summary is not an indication that a
particular finding is not based in part on that fact.

SECTION 15: Reliance On Record. Each and every one of the findings and determination
in this Resolution are based on the competent and substantial evidence, both oral and
written, contained in the entire record relating to the project. The findings and
determinations constitute the independent findings and determinations of the City Council
in all respects and are fully and completely supported by substantial evidence in the
record as a whole.

SECTION 16: Severability. If any part of this Ordinance or its application is deemed invalid
by a court of competent jurisdiction, the City Council intends that such invalidity will not
affect the effectiveness of the remaining provisions or applications and, to this end, the
provisions of this Ordinance are severable.

SECTION 17: Preservation. This Resolution does not affect any penalty, forfeiture, or
liability incurred before, or prelude prosecution and imposition of penalties for any
violation occurring before, this Resolution’s effective date. Any such amended part will

  MISSION STATEMENT
  The mission of the City of Monterey Park is to provide excellent service, foster growth
  and opportunity, and create a joyous and collaborative environment.

  LAND ACKNOWLEDGMENT
  We would like to acknowledge that the land we inhabit today was once known as
  Tovangaar, the home of the Gabrieleño-Tongva people. We show our respect to the
  Gabrieleño-Tongva people, as well as all Indigenous people, past, present, and future,
  and honor their labor as original caretakers of this land. We commit to uplifting the
  Gabrieleño-Tongva people, invite you to acknowledge the history, and join us in caring
  for this land.

GENERAL INFORMATION
Documents related to an Agenda item are available to the public in the City Clerk’s Office located at 320
West Newmark Avenue, Monterey Park, CA 91754, during normal business hours and the City’s website
at www.montereypark.ca.gov/AgendaCenter/City-Council-17.

The public may watch the meeting live on the city’s cable channel MPKTV (AT&T U-verse, channel 99
or Charter Communications, channel 182) or by visiting the city’s website at
www.montereypark.ca.gov/133/City-Council-Meeting-Videos. Per the Americans with Disabilities Act, if
you need special assistance to participate in this meeting, please call City Hall at (626) 307-1359 for
reasonable accommodation at least 24 hours before a meeting. Council Chambers are wheelchair
accessible.

PUBLIC PARTICIPATION

another person’s speaking. No person may speak more than a total of 10 minutes. The Mayor and City
Council may change the amount of time allowed for speakers. Written Communication will be accepted
up  to  24  hours  before  the  meeting  by  completing  an  online  form  at
www.montereypark.ca.gov/writtencomm.

item not on the agenda. The Council may briefly respond to comments after Public Communications is
closed. Persons may, in addition to any other matter within the City Council's subject-matter jurisdiction,
comment on Agenda Items at this time. If you provide public comment on a specific Agenda item at this
time, however, you cannot later provide comments at the time the Agenda Item is considered.
